name: Embodied posture feedback (self-validation)

lead: Embodied posture feedback is the idea that the body's posture feeds back into the mind. Sitting or standing tall and open is said to make a person feel more confident and sure of their own thoughts, and that confidence then shows in how they move, speak and present themselves.

For looks, the appeal is that posture is free and immediate: an upright frame reads as taller, broader and more self-assured. A 2009 line of research by Briñol, Petty and Wagner proposed a 'self-validation' mechanism, and the related power-posing research (2010 onward) examined brief expansive poses. A 2022 meta-analysis reported a reliable effect on feelings such as dominance and mood, with no physiological effect.

paras: Practitioners hold an upright, open posture (shoulders back, chest open, head level) in daily life or for a short period before a social or professional situation, often alongside posture-correction exercises.
No direct risks are reported for adopting an upright posture. Forcing an exaggerated posture can be uncomfortable, and researchers note that claims about hormone changes were not reproduced.

chain: Carry and present yourself with more presence
angle.text: Upright posture directly changes how tall and broad a person looks, and proponents say it also changes how confident they feel, which affects body language and presence. Research supports the feeling-of-power part of that chain more than hormonal or behavioural claims.

lead: Embodied posture feedback is the proposal that body posture influences how a person feels and thinks about themselves, so that standing or sitting upright and expansively increases confidence and confidence-linked presentation. In looksmaxxing discussions it is used as one reason to work on posture: an upright stance changes apparent height, shoulder width and neck-jaw line, and is also said to change the person's own demeanour.

The research behind it comes from two overlapping traditions. In the 2010 paper by Carney, Cuddy and Yap, brief high-power poses were reported to raise testosterone, lower cortisol and increase risk-taking; Amy Cuddy's 2012 TED talk popularised the idea.[1] A related account, self-validation, holds that posture can make people more confident in their own thoughts. Embodied cognition research more broadly has studied how posture and facial movement affect emotion and attitudes.[2]

Later replication work found different results by outcome. A larger 2015 study by Ranehill and colleagues confirmed an effect on felt power but not on hormones or behaviour, and in 2016 Carney published a statement saying she no longer believed the effects were real.[1] A 2022 meta-analysis of 128 studies reported a reliable effect on thoughts and feelings such as mood and dominance, but none on physiology.[1]
infobox: Effect on felt power, not hormones[1]

paras: Embodied (or embodied-cognition) accounts say mental states are shaped in part by the body. Researchers have reported that adopting postures linked with fear, anger or sadness modulated the emotion people experienced, and that nodding while hearing a message produced more positive attitudes toward it than head-shaking.[2]

Applied to appearance, the claim is simple: an upright, open posture makes someone feel more confident and be seen as more confident. Proponents of posture work in looksmaxxing communities describe this as a loop in which better posture improves self-image and self-image improves posture.

The 2010 power-posing paper reported hormone and risk-taking changes after two minutes in expansive poses.[1] Subsequent studies by Ranehill (2015), Garrison (2016), Deuter (2016) and Smith (2017) did not find hormonal or behavioural changes.[1] In 2016 Simmons and Simonsohn argued that the pool of studies showed no effect after accounting for selective reporting, while Cuddy and colleagues' 2017-2018 meta-analysis of 55 studies reported effects on emotional and affective states.[1]
A 2022 meta-analysis of 128 studies found a reliable effect on thoughts and feelings but no physiological effect, and said the behavioural effect remained unclear.[1]

The research consists of laboratory psychology experiments rather than clinical trials. Reported findings are summarised above: effects on felt power and mood in meta-analyses, and no reproducible hormonal effect.[1]
